title: Stress Lives in the Appraisal
objective: After this level you can explain how the way you judge a demand and your resources shapes how stressful it feels.
summary: In Lazarus and Folkman's view, stress follows appraisal: judging a threat or challenge, then your resources. A 1964 film study showed a new framing changes the body's stress response.

cards.headline: Same event, different stress. The difference is in your head.
cards.body: Two people can face the same bad news and react very differently. Psychologists Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman explained why: stress is a process in which people respond to events they appraise, or judge, as overwhelming or threatening. So what exactly are we judging?

cards.headline: Two quick judgments
cards.body: First comes a primary appraisal: how much harm or threat does this hold? The same event can be seen as a threat, a possible loss, or as a challenge, a chance to gain or grow. Then comes a secondary appraisal: what options do I have to cope, and how well will they work? A job interview can feel like a threat or a challenge depending on how you answer both.

cards.headline: When demands outrun resources
cards.body: Put the two together and you get the core rule: people feel stressed when they judge an event as harmful and believe its demands exceed their resources to handle it. Not all stress is bad, though. Eustress is good stress that motivates performance; distress is stress so excessive that performance declines. The same exam can push one student and flatten another.

cards.headline: Change the story, change the body
cards.body: Lazarus tested the idea in the lab. In a 1964 study led by Joseph Speisman, people watched the same stressful film with different soundtracks. A soundtrack that stressed the threat raised their skin conductance, a bodily sign of stress. Soundtracks that offered calmer interpretations lowered it. Same film, different appraisal, different body.

mascot.line: This is Level 6's idea at work: the mind processes information, and how it reads an event shapes what happens next.

cards.headline: Stress and appraisal
learned: Primary appraisal: how threatening is this?
Stress when demands seem to exceed resources
A new framing lowered bodily stress in a 1964 study

questions.prompt: In Lazarus and Folkman's model, what does the secondary appraisal judge?

options.label: Whether the event happened at all
options.rationale: Both appraisals assume the event is real.

options.label: How much harm or threat the event holds
The options for coping and how well they'll work
Whether other people are also stressed
options.rationale: The model focuses on your own judgments.

questions.explanation: The secondary appraisal weighs your options for coping and how effective they will be.

questions.prompt: Maya and Tom face the same deadline. Maya thinks, "I can plan this." Tom thinks, "There's no way I can manage." Who likely feels more stressed?

options.label: Maya, because she sees more work ahead
options.rationale: Seeing a plan means she judges her resources as enough.

options.label: Tom, because he judges the demands exceed his resources
Both equally, because the deadline is the same
options.rationale: Appraisal, not the event alone, shapes stress.

options.label: Neither, because deadlines cause only eustress
options.rationale: Deadlines can bring eustress or distress.

questions.explanation: Stress follows when demands seem to exceed resources. Tom's appraisal fits that; Maya judges she can cope.

questions.prompt: Level 6's cognitive revolution asked what happens between a signal going in and behavior coming out. What does the 1964 film study suggest happens there?

options.label: Nothing: the film alone set the stress level
options.rationale: The same film gave different stress with different soundtracks.

options.label: The mind interprets the event, and that shapes the stress
Only rewards and punishments shape the reaction
Stress depends only on how long the film lasts
options.rationale: Length was the same; the framing changed.

questions.explanation: The same film caused more or less bodily stress depending on how the soundtrack framed it, so the mind's interpretation sits between input and response.
